extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and evaluating whether patent claims recite an abstract idea (judicial exception) and whether additional claim elements integrate that idea into a patent-eligible practical application (Step 2A Prong One/Two and Step 2B under §101).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish claims 'directed to' a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus distinguishes claims that are “directed to” the recited judicial exception from claims that are not “directed to” the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judicial exception is not eligible subject matter; if a claim is directed to the judicial exception it requires further analysis under the Alice/Mayo framework. If a claim contains only the judicial exception (or merely recites another judicial exception), it is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application and is not eligible. Examiners should make appropriate rejections (see MPEP § 2106.07) and it is a best practice to recommend an amendment that would resolve eligibility if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional elements must 'transform' exception into patent-eligible application
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements (if any) in the claim must “transform into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception, either at Prong Two or in Step 2B.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are no additional elements in the claim, then it cannot be eligible. If additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient (e.g., adding one abstract idea to another does not render the claim non-abstract). Examiners should evaluate whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend amendment when claim lacks additional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are no additional elements in the claim, then it cannot be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After making the appropriate rejection (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating a rejection for lack of eligibility), it is a best practice for the examiner to recommend an amendment, if possible, that would resolve eligibility of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply same eligibility analysis regardless of number of exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis to all claims regardless of the number of exceptions recited therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless it is clear a claim recites distinct exceptions (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas. If possible, treat the claim for Prong Two and Step 2B purposes as containing a single judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: When exceptions are distinct, select one exception to analyze
rubrics_metrics.description: In some claims, the multiple exceptions are distinct from each other (e.g., a first limitation describes a law of nature and a second limitation recites an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For examination efficiency, examiners should select one of the exceptions and conduct the eligibility analysis for that selected exception. If the analysis indicates the claim recites additional element(s) that integrate the selected exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more than the selected exception, then consider the claim patent eligible. If not, consider the claim ineligible. (See University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not parse multiple abstract ideas; consider together when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: In claims reciting multiple abstract ideas (same or different groupings) or multiple laws of nature, examiners should not parse the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify multiple concepts (e.g., mental steps and mathematical calculation) in Step 2A Prong One to make the record clear, but where possible consider the limitations together as a single abstract idea for Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B rather than analyzing separate abstract ideas individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use enumerated groupings to identify abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office has set forth an approach to identifying abstract ideas that distills case law into enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shifts examiners away from a pure case-comparison approach toward generally applying a body of case law across technologies. The enumerated groupings are: (1) Mathematical concepts; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) Mental processes. See MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) for further discussion of groupings and their relation to precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify specific claim limitations that recite an abstract idea (two-step identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim under examination that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas listed above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the identified limitation(s) fall within a grouping, reasonable to conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and the claim then requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application. If the identified limitations do not fall within any of the groupings, reasonable to find the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the analysis concludes at Pathway B, unless the claim recites another exception (e.g., law of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: If limitation falls within a grouping -> proceed to Step 2A Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: If the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude that the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim then requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether any additional elements in the claim integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: If limitation does not fall within any grouping -> eligible at Pathway B
rubrics_metrics.description: If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any of the groupings of abstract ideas, it is reasonable to find that the claim does not recite an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concludes the abstract idea judicial exception eligibility analysis (Pathway B), except in rare circumstances discussed in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3). The claim is thus eligible at Pathway B unless it recites and is directed to another exception (such as a law of nature or natural phenomenon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Groupings are not mutually exclusive; identify all applicable groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: The groupings of abstract ideas are not mutually exclusive; some claims recite limitations that fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify at least one abstract idea grouping, but preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a claim limitation is determined to fall within multiple groupings, and proceed with the analysis in Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reciting an abstract idea from merely involving one (Prong One caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: While all inventions at some level embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract ideas, not all claims recite an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Step 2A Prong One analysis requires a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in Prong One before proceeding to the Prong Two inquiry about whether the claim is directed to that idea, thereby separating claims that recite abstract ideas from those that merely are based on or involve an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting hypotheticals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea include specific device or method claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples provided: (i) a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead, and ink cartridge; (ii) a washing machine with tub, drive motor, controller and housing; (iii) an earring with a glucose sensor and memory; (iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences (amplify and sequence); (v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system from remote memory; (vi) a method of rearranging icons on a GUI based on usage; (vii) a method of training a neural network with staged training sets. These examples show claims that do not recite abstract ideas and are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts grouping definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematical concepts grouping is defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified many concepts within this grouping (e.g., converting binary-coded decimal, Arrhenius equation, mathematical formula for hedging). When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, consider whether the claim recites the mathematical concept or merely limitations that are based on or involve it. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept may not fall into the grouping if the mathematical concept itself is not recited in the claim. Mathematical concepts need not be expressed in symbols; words operating on data can serve the same purpose (e.g., “determining a ratio of A to B”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships indicators and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers and may be expressed in words or using mathematical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (i) relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Arrhenius equation); (ii) conversion between binary-coded decimal and pure binary; (iii) relationship between radio activity and antenna conductor arrangement; (iv) organizing/manipulating information through mathematical correlations. If a claim recites such relationships it likely falls in the mathematical concepts grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations indicators and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a numerical formula or equation will be considered as falling within the “mathematical concepts” grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual expressions of formulas (e.g., “determining a ratio of A to B” or “calculating force by multiplying mass by acceleration”) also count. Examples: electromagnetic standing wave formulas; the Arrhenius equation; a formula for computing an alarm limit; a mathematical formula for hedging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations indicators and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a mathematical calculation, when given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification, will be considered as falling within the “mathematical concepts” grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical calculation means performing a mathematical operation or using mathematical methods to determine a variable or number (e.g., determining, performing, calculating). Examples include resampled statistical analysis to generate distribution, calculating an alarm limit, converting geospatial coordinates, managing insurance policy values via calculations, algorithms for optimization, and calculating differences between local and average values.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Certain methods of organizing human activity’ grouping definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase “methods of organizing human activity” describes concepts relating to: (i) fundamental economic principles or practices; (ii) commercial or legal interactions; and (iii) managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term “certain” limits the grouping: not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas (e.g., a defined set of steps for combining ingredients to create a drug formulation is not). The sub-groupings encompass both single-person activity and multi-person interactions, and activity between a person and a computer may fall within this grouping. The grouping should not be expanded beyond the enumerated sub-groupings except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices examples and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental economic principles or practices include hedging, insurance, and mitigating risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Fundamental’ does not mean necessarily old; new methods can be fundamental economic concepts. Examples: hedging (Bilski), mitigating settlement risk (Alice), rules for wagering games, financial instruments protecting against investment risk, offer-based price optimization, local processing of payments for remote purchases. Such concepts have been treated as abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions examples and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or legal interactions include agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where claims were held directed to such interactions: transaction performance guaranty (buySAFE), aggregating real property into portfolios and deedshares (legal obligation example), processing insurance claims (Accenture/Guidewire), using advertising as exchange for copyrighted media (Ultramercial). These activities, when claimed at an abstract level (e.g., creating contractual relationships, using advertising as currency), are likely within this subgroup.
